method: Sources were inspected first and pages written from what the passages state. No page was created before its evidence existed.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 5: Gamma Function
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter title and DLMF release 1.2.7, dated 2026-06-15, confirmed on the chapter page before the sections were read.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: 5.5.3 reflection formula with its excluded points
5.11.1 Stirling expansion with its sector of validity

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The gamma function is fixed by a recurrence, and two further relations carry an argument across the half-plane and between scales.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 5.5.1 states Gamma(z+1) equals z times Gamma(z). 5.5.3 states Gamma(z) times Gamma(1-z) equals pi over sin(pi z), for z not zero and not a negative integer. 5.5.5 states the duplication formula, Gamma(2z) equals pi to the minus one half, times 2 to the power 2z-1, times Gamma(z) times Gamma(z+1/2), for 2z not zero and not a negative integer.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Large arguments are handled by an expansion that is asymptotic rather than convergent, so accuracy is bounded by the smallest term rather than by the number of terms taken.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 5.11.1 gives the Stirling series for the logarithm of Gamma(z) as z tends to infinity in the sector where the phase of z is at most pi minus delta. The relation is written with the asymptotic symbol, which the chapter identifies as a Poincare asymptotic expansion rather than a convergent series. 5.11.2 gives the corresponding expansion for the digamma function under the same sector condition.

inspected.establishes: The functional relations that define and compute the gamma function, each with the conditions the reference attaches to it.
inspected.boundary: States identities at their declared scope. It does not establish that any implementation attains a stated accuracy, and an asymptotic expansion carries no error bound from the term count alone.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 7: Error Function, Dawson Integral, and Fresnel Integrals
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapter 5.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The error function and its complement are defined as normalised integrals of the Gaussian kernel, and the two are related by a stated identity.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 7.2.1 defines erf z as two over the square root of pi, times the integral of exp of minus t squared from zero to z. 7.2.2 defines erfc z as the same normalised integral taken from z to infinity, and states in the same equation that erfc z equals one minus erf z.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The chapter defines the Dawson and Fresnel integrals alongside the error function, and records all of them as entire functions.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 7.2.5 defines the Dawson integral F(z) as exp of minus z squared times the integral of exp of t squared from zero to z. 7.2.7 and 7.2.8 define the Fresnel integrals C(z) and S(z) as the integrals of cosine and sine of pi t squared over two. The chapter records these as entire functions of the complex variable.

inspected.establishes: Integral definitions for the error function, its complement, the Dawson integral and the Fresnel integrals, with the identity relating erf and erfc.
inspected.boundary: Defines the functions and their relations. It does not establish the accuracy of any implementation, and no statistical interpretation follows from a definition.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 10: Bessel Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapters 5 and 7.
exactLocators: 10.2.1 the differential equation and its singularity structure

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The equation has a stated singularity structure, and its first-kind solution is a series whose coefficients are gamma values.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 10.2.1 states the equation as z squared w double prime plus z w prime plus the quantity z squared minus nu squared times w equals zero, and records that it has a regular singularity at z equals zero with indices plus and minus nu and an irregular singularity of rank one at infinity. 10.2.2 gives the first-kind solution as a power series in which the k-th coefficient divides by the gamma function at nu plus k plus one, and notes it is analytic except for a branch point at the origin when nu is not an integer.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The second solution is constructed from the first and degenerates at integer order, and choosing a pair is a question of region rather than of independence alone.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 10.2.3 builds the second-kind solution from first-kind solutions of order plus and minus nu, divided by sine of nu pi. 10.2.4 supplies the limiting form at integer order where that construction degenerates. The chapter records that the second-kind solution has a branch point at the origin whether or not nu is an integer, with a cut along the negative reals, and Table 10.2.1 tabulates which pairs are numerically satisfactory in which region.

inspected.establishes: The Bessel equation, its singularity structure, both standard solutions, and which pairs are numerically satisfactory by region.
inspected.boundary: States the solutions and their analytic structure. It does not select a pair for a given computation, and makes no accuracy claim about any implementation.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 24: Bernoulli and Euler Polynomials
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapters 5, 7 and 10.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The Bernoulli numbers and polynomials are defined by generating functions that converge only inside a stated disk.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 24.2.1 defines the Bernoulli numbers by t over the quantity e to the t minus one, expanded as a sum of B sub n times t to the n over n factorial, stated to converge for the modulus of t less than two pi. 24.2.3 gives the polynomials from the same expression multiplied by e to the x t in the same disk, and 24.2.4 records that B sub n equals B sub n of zero.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Odd-indexed coefficients vanish apart from one exception, and the Euler generating function converges in a strictly smaller disk than the Bernoulli one.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 24.2.2 states that odd-indexed Bernoulli numbers vanish apart from the first, and that the even ones alternate in sign with minus one to the n plus one times B sub two n positive for n at least one. 24.2.6 defines the Euler numbers by two e to the t over the quantity e to the two t plus one, converging only for the modulus of t less than pi over two, and 24.2.7 states that odd-indexed Euler numbers vanish.

inspected.crossPageNote: The vanishing rule at 24.2.2 explains a feature of the gamma page: the Stirling expansion at 5.11.1 is indexed by even numbers because the odd Bernoulli coefficients are zero. Both halves of that observation are inspected.
inspected.establishes: Generating-function definitions with their convergence radii, and the vanishing and sign rules for odd and even indices.
inspected.boundary: Defines the coefficients inside stated disks. It makes no claim about the numerical stability of any recurrence used to generate them.

inspected.title: Asteroseismology Using The Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey
inspected.identifier: science.nasa.gov Roman Space Telescope survey description
inspected.identityBasis: Publisher and page title confirmed on retrieval.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government agency publication, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: Properties measured for tens of thousands of stars

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The observable is a long, regularly sampled photometric series, from which an oscillation frequency pattern is characterised.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that the approach relies on precise, regularly sampled, long-duration photometric observations to characterise the oscillation frequency pattern of evolved red giants, which it describes as high-amplitude non-radial oscillators.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Masses, radii and ages are inferred only in combination with separately measured metallicity and temperature, and saturation remains an open constraint.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that masses, radii and ages have been measured for tens of thousands of stars using asteroseismic data combined with stellar metallicity and effective temperature. It also states that saturation will be important for red clump stars in the Galactic bulge, and describes an improved asteroseismic detection model including the effect of saturation as work to be developed.

inspected.notCovered: The page does not explain why the oscillations occur, and gives no frequencies, amplitudes or precision figures. The page built on it therefore records the driving mechanism as unestablished and makes no numerical accuracy claim.
inspected.establishes: The asteroseismic observable, the properties inferred from it in combination with other measurements, and the saturation constraint the survey still faces.
inspected.boundary: A mission survey description. It establishes the method's inputs and outputs, not the physics behind them or any precision figure.

heldBack.identityBasis: Publisher and page title confirmed on retrieval.
heldBack.rightsBasis: United States government agency publication, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: The named detection methods and what each measures
The stated limitation on radial velocity detections
The stated limitation on direct imaging
heldBack.partialCoverage: The page's line naming astrometry, microlensing, timing and direct imaging together is only partly covered. NASA names microlensing and direct imaging but not astrometry or timing, so that line is not claimed as supported.
heldBack.establishes: Which detection methods NASA names, what each measures, and the selection biases it states for two of them.
heldBack.boundary: An agency overview. It does not establish the sensitivity or completeness of any survey, and it states limitations for only some of the methods it names.
heldBack.notAttachedReason: Inspected at section level and ready to attach, but held back. The route it supports, /knowledge/astronomy/exoplanet-detection-and-confirmation, is one of the twenty records in the Phase 4 pilot, whose manifest carries a frozen sha256. That manifest is recomputed from live data rather than stored, so adding any source to a pilot record moves the digest: this source took the blocker count from 87 to 89. Every existing astronomy source carries the same two blockers, a missing publication date and a missing locator, so the source is no worse than its neighbours; the coupling is the issue. Updating a frozen release-governance digest to accommodate a content addition is a decision for a person, not a side effect of adding a page.
